name: Pierluca D'Oro
bio: Pierluca D’Oro is founder at a stealth startup revolutionizing how humans interact with AI-generated software. At Mila, he pioneered two early ideas that now sit at the center of agent development: making reinforcement learning scale through simple recipes, and using LLMs as feedback systems to train agents. At Meta Superintelligence Labs, he worked on frontier model development and led environment generation for mobile computer use agents.

positions.claim: A replay agent that blindly replays recorded action sequences achieves the same or better success rate than the frontier model it was extracted from on standard benchmarks like OSWorld and Mobile World.
Pass@k evaluated on a deterministic environment is formally equivalent to measuring the success rate of a replay agent, making it an inappropriate metric for computer-use tasks.
Static, deterministic benchmarks are inherently gameable and should be replaced by multifactorial environments that vary data, appearance, and initial state.
No existing computer-use benchmark satisfies all five PRISM environment-design principles simultaneously.
DigWorld comprises 15 Android apps, 387 verified scenarios, and 3.2 million verified configurations.
The bottleneck in building diverse environments is not generating software with coding agents but verifying that generated configurations are valid.
Most frontier models are not robust to variations in starting screen or app theme, despite performing well on the base version of the same task.
Confidence intervals computed from rollouts alone achieve only about 17-20% empirical coverage instead of the nominal 95%.
Accounting for the hierarchical structure of the benchmark when computing confidence intervals restores coverage to the nominal 90-95%.
Overconfident confidence intervals can cause model-deployment mistakes costing hundreds of thousands of dollars per month at a scale of one million tasks with a 4% true performance gap.
Varying the initial state across runs is rare in existing benchmarks but should be standard practice in evals.
Continuing to use a known-gameable benchmark harms the field by directing optimization toward scores that do not capture what practitioners care about.
A benchmark is adequately de-gamed only if a replay agent extracted from it scores near zero on it.
